Title: El Niño 2026: How Big Could It Get?
Location: Hogan Hall, Room Hogan A, 566 W 114th St (+ Zoom)
Host: Center for Climate Systems Research, Columbia Climate School
Why go: The quarterly ENSO briefing from the people who make the forecast: how strong this gets, and which regions face drought, floods, and heat next.
Summary: Center for Climate Systems Research (Columbia Climate School) ENSO and Climate Quarterly Briefing on the rapidly strengthening 2026 El Niño: the latest ENSO observations and forecasts as it approaches peak intensity, and which regions face heightened risk of drought, heavy rainfall, flooding, heat, and other extremes in the coming seasons. The science companion to Columbia's Beyond the Forecast panel the next day. Open to the public, in person or on Zoom via the event page.

Title: A Postcard from the Future: The Heat Toll of the 2026-27 Super El Niño and What We Can Still Do
Location: Glasshouse on Bryant Park, 9th Floor, 54 W 40th St
Host: University of Chicago Institute for Climate & Sustainable Growth, with C2ES
Why go: First look at Climate Impact Lab's projection of how many people this El Niño's heat could kill, where, and what still saves lives.
Summary: University of Chicago Institute for Climate & Sustainable Growth session, co-hosted by C2ES, previewing a forthcoming Climate Impact Lab report projecting how many people could die from this El Niño's record heat, concentrated in the countries least able to adapt and with the thinnest warning systems. Frames El Niño as a postcard from the future: a preview of temperatures expected to become normal under climate change. Covers the scale of projected deaths, where they concentrate, and what can still be done globally and within countries and communities to save lives. Speakers: Michael Greenstone, Nat Keohane, Michelle Nunn, Hari Menon, Greg Puley. Public; register via Cvent (https://web.cvent.com/event/a4ca007d-3993-45ed-87bb-3446ccbbe55c/register).

Title: Beyond the Forecast: What El Niño Reveals About Science, Society, and Action
Location: The Forum at Columbia University, Auditorium, 601 W 125th St
Why go: What happens after the forecast: why people and institutions act on the same warning so differently, and what makes a community ready.
Summary: Columbia Climate School panel of its Climate, Earth, and Society Distinguished Fellows on what happens after an El Niño forecast is made: how people, institutions, and communities respond to climate information, and why readiness lags what scientists can see months ahead. Dean Alexis Abramson opens; Senior Vice Dean Jeffrey Shaman gives a scientific overview of El Niño and moderates; Fellows Justin Brice Guariglia (visual artist and environmental storyteller) and Mareva Grabowski-Mitsotakis (entrepreneur, sustainable business and cultural preservation) discuss. Program 2:00 to 3:00pm with audience Q&A, reception 3:00 to 3:30pm. Hosted by Columbia Climate School; register via the Columbia event page.

Title: Frontline Resilience: Adapting Smallholder Agriculture to El Niño & Extreme Climate
Why go: How El Niño is hitting smallholder farmers in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and what agribusiness is doing to keep those supply chains standing.
Summary: Climate Action for Smallholders Coalition panel on how El Niño is reshaping smallholder farming communities across Africa, Asia, and Latin America; how global agribusinesses are investing in smallholders to secure resilient supply chains; and how pairing digital extension tools with on-the-ground technical assistance and market access speeds adaptation. Speakers: Elizabeth Teague, Katherine Georges, Whitney Kakos, Eric Firnhaber, Tracy Bain. Public; register via HubSpot form (https://share.hsforms.com/1rLqCKiFsTwOSmSdFybXeyQqnt1q).

Title: NYPH Regenerative Metropolis Symposium 2026
Why go: A full day on buildings that hold up, whose hosts have promised El Niño two minutes from the main microphone.
Summary: New York Passive House's annual symposium, on the official Climate Week NYC program: a full day on regenerative design, systems thinking, and regenerative economics in the built environment, starting from Passive House principles. Keynotes on regenerative economics, sessions on business models and sustainable construction, bioregional case studies, a working lunch, and an evening networking reception. Open to students, architects, engineers, developers, contractors, manufacturers, policymakers, owners, advocates, and the public. Registration via the NYPH members site.

Title: 10th NYC Green School Conference 2026
Location: SUNY Global Center, 116 East 55th Street, New York, NY 10022
Why go: A decade-old global green education conference during UNGA week, whose hosts promised El Nino two minutes from the main microphone.
Summary: Green Mentors hosts this two-day conference on September 23 and 24, 2026, convened during Climate Week NYC and alongside the 81st UN General Assembly. The published program runs plenaries, keynotes, policy dialogues, youth research presentations and campus sustainability sessions, closing with the Global Green Awards 2026 ceremony on day two. It is aimed at educators, school and university leaders, policymakers, researchers, students, governments, international organizations, corporate leaders and investors. Attendance requires registration through the conference website; the listed delegate rate is $500 USD with a 50 percent student waiver, and the site states a registration deadline of September 15, 2026. A separate free two-day Global Classroom 2026 track for university and college student groups runs in parallel on the same dates.
